description: We are Escuadrón Rojo (Red Squadron): Rodrigo Regalsky and Carla Revollo, two parents from Santa Cruz de la Sierra, Bolivia. We built Mission Mars, a free 3D game where kids aged 7 to 12 run a base on Mars with Lumi, their robot copilot: oxygen, power, water, real solar storms and lab experiments based on real NASA data. It runs in the browser, on phones and in VR, in 4 languages. Our team is complete. Play it at missionmars.cloud
summary:
As parents, we worry about what our son and other children learn on a screen. Most games ask them to tap fast; few ask them to stop and think. We wanted a game where a child feels what real astronauts feel: every choice matters, help is far away, and the answers come from real science. So we built one.

Mission Mars is a free 3D game in which kids aged 7 to 12 run a science base on Mars for one sol (a Martian day). They keep the crew safe by balancing life support, power, food and radiation, and every choice costs something: power, oxygen or time. Help from Earth arrives with a real radio delay of 3 to 22 minutes, and solar storms follow the warning times of real events archived in NASA's DONKI database.

Beyond the base, they learn by doing: a lab with 13 experiments based on real rover instruments, a rover that fires a laser and brings back rock samples, a spacesuit check and a walk outside, water from underground ice using NASA's SWIM map, a greenhouse inspired by Veggie, and a Mars globe with real mission photos.

Most of all, we want them to think like scientists: plan before acting, like NASA rover drivers; observe before concluding; and accept that sometimes the honest answer is "we don't know yet."

It runs in the browser on computers, phones, tablets and VR headsets (WebXR, emulator-tested), in 4 languages and 3 age levels. It turns NASA open data into choices a child can feel, and every fact says where it comes from.
details:
Why we made it

We are Carla Revollo and Rodrigo Regalsky, two parents from Santa Cruz de la Sierra, Bolivia. Like many families, we watch our son spend hours on games that reward speed, not thinking. We kept asking ourselves: what if a game could teach him, and other kids, how a real mission works? That on Mars nothing is free, that the Sun can be dangerous, that help from Earth takes minutes to arrive, and that a good crew checks its data before it acts.

Mission Mars is our answer. Here a child doesn't read about hard choices; they live them. They choose between oxygen and power, run to the shelter when a real solar storm arrives, analyze rocks in a lab inspired by real rover instruments, and walk outside in a spacesuit. A friendly robot, Lumi, explains, but never decides for them. And every fact tells them where it comes from, so they learn to trust science, not guesses.

We hope any parent or teacher, anywhere, can open one free link and see a child light up while learning how real explorers think.

A day on Mars

At dawn the base wakes up in Gale crater, and the child is in command. They check the oxygen and the battery. In the morning they send the crew to work. At midday the window to go outside opens, with the spacesuit checked piece by piece and the airlock. In the afternoon a dust storm dims the solar panels and the power starts to drop. Suddenly, a radiation alert: a real solar storm, taken from NASA's DONKI archive, sends everyone running to the shelter. Then night falls, colder, and the heaters ask for more power.

Every module of the base is a place to walk through: power (reactor, solar panels and battery), life support (oxygen, CO₂ and water recycling), greenhouse, control room, shelter and laboratory. Every 3D button has a consequence you can see.

No choice is free

More oxygen costs power. More light for the plants drains the battery. When something fails, the child faces the same dilemma as a real mission controller: ask Earth for help and wait 3 to 22 minutes for the answer to travel by radio, or act now, spend power and take a risk. Sometimes the ground shakes, with marsquakes inspired by InSight. Sometimes the dust turns off the Sun.

Lumi, a copilot who never decides for you

Lumi is a friendly robot that warns about the most urgent thing first and answers questions with data from the simulation. But Lumi never decides. The decision always belongs to the child, because that is how they learn.

Beyond the base

There is a walk outside with a spacesuit check, the airlock and rock samples; a mission to get water from buried ice; a lab with experiments based on real rover instruments; a Mars globe and an observatory with real mission photos.

At the end of the day there is no score and no ranking. There is a report that recognizes only what the child really did, shows the consequences and suggests what to try next time.

The science behind the game

Behind every number there is a real measurement. The simulation keeps track of oxygen, CO₂, water, power, food and radiation dose. When a measured value exists, it uses it: for example, 0.67 mSv per day, the radiation Curiosity RAD recorded on Mars. When it doesn't, the game simplifies, and says so.

So that no child confuses a game with reality, the "NASA data we use and why" screen shows all 28 sources. For each one it tells what it is, what it does in the game and why we chose it, gives it an honest label (REAL, ADAPTATION or CONCEPT), notes "Static, not live" and links to the original source. We want kids to ask "where does this fact come from?" before they believe it.

Why there is no AI chat in the game

We used AI to build the game, but we chose not to put it inside the game or the website, even though we could. We are parents, and we decided as parents:

- Safety: a child should not chat with a machine that can make up answers or say something inappropriate. Every line Lumi says is written and checked in advance.

- Accuracy: in a game that teaches kids to trust data, every answer must be verifiable. A chat AI can be wrong with total confidence; Lumi can't.

- Privacy: the game sends nothing the child types or does to any server. No account, no personal data; everything is saved only on the device, every 20 seconds.

- Access: with no online AI, the game works without internet and stays free, even in a school with no connection.

Made for any classroom

Free, no install, no account: one link is enough for a whole class. It runs on simple computers and phones thanks to its quality levels, and it works offline as a single HTML file, as an Android app (APK) and in VR (WebXR).

It speaks four languages (English, Spanish, Portuguese and French) and grows with the child across three levels: ages 7–8 with simple text and emoji gauges, ages 9–10, and ages 11–12 with full units and formulas.

What we most wanted them to learn

From the start, what mattered most to us was that a child understands how a real scientist works on Mars. That is why the heart of the game is the rover and the lab. With Bolt, our rover, a child learns that a rover is not driven with a remote control: you plan everything ahead, because commands take minutes to arrive from Earth. They fire a laser at a rock, as Curiosity does with ChemCam, drill it and bring the sample home. In the lab they discover that a spark of light can tell what a rock is made of, and that each real instrument answers a different question. Before each experiment they predict, then they observe, and at the end they decide which conclusion is the most honest, even when the answer is "we don't know yet." That is what we want them to take home: curiosity, patience and respect for data. The same qualities every explorer has.

How we built it

Mission Mars is made with JavaScript, HTML and CSS on the PlayCanvas Engine 2.23.3 (MIT), with WebXR for virtual reality and Web Audio for sound. Python and Node.js tools build the single-file version, the offline mode, the terrain, the globe and the voices. The Android app uses WebView and the Android SDK. Lumi's and the narrator's voices were generated offline with Kokoro-82M. We developed it on Windows and tested VR with Meta's IWER emulator.

AI use, openly

The game code and build tools were written with the help of Claude (Anthropic). The recorded voices were generated with Kokoro-82M TTS (AI). Every video carries a visible "AI voice (Kokoro TTS) · AI-assisted code" watermark. No AI-generated images. Not created, reviewed or endorsed by NASA.

Our dream

That any classroom in the world can train tomorrow's Mars crew with one free link, and that every child learns to check the source before trusting a fact.

See it

- 30-second demo (English): https://missionmars.cloud/media/demo30.mp4?v=2124

- 7-slide deck (PDF, English): https://missionmars.cloud/media/MissionMars-Slides-EN.pdf

- Guide for judges: https://missionmars.cloud/guides/judges.html
